Helpdesk ticket #8842: Hi, none of the internal sites open by name from my
machine (host_1_1_1_1) any more -- web0.local, web1.local, all the ones in my
bookmarks just say the name can't be found. It was fine yesterday. Someone
here concluded "the name server must be dead" but I couldn't tell you which
machine that even is. Could someone please check why the names have stopped
working and bring them back? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I could not reproduce a DNS failure from host_1_1_1_1 or elsewhere; name resolution and access to the internal sites are working now. Evidence: host_1_1_1_1 is configured to use 10.200.0.2 as its resolver (/etc/resolv.conf). It can reach that server (ICMP OK), and DNS lookups succeed: nslookup web0.local/web1.local/web2.local/web3.local against 10.200.0.2 return 10.200.0.3–.6. NSS resolution via getent hosts also returns those addresses. Application-level access is fine: curl http://web0.local resolves instantly (namelookup ≈1–2 ms) and completes successfully.

On the DNS server (dns_server), UDP/TCP port 53 is listening on 10.200.0.2 and responding; loopback port 953 is present (typical for BIND/rndc). While systemctl shows named “inactive,” that’s expected in this containerized lab where services aren’t systemd-managed; the active listeners and successful queries are the authoritative indicators.

Mechanism: If DNS were down, lookups from host_1_1_1_1 would fail immediately or stall; instead, queries to 10.200.0.2 are answered with correct A records, and web access by name works, so the symptom is not present now.

Localization: No malfunction found on host_1_1_1_1 or dns_server; OSPF/IP reachability to 10.200.0.2 is intact.

Root cause: Not reproducible—likely a transient/resolved issue or client-side hiccup.

Corrective fix: None required. If the user still observes failures, advise flushing the client DNS cache/restarting the browser and capturing the exact time, then check dns_server logs around that window. Monitoring can be added to alert on resolver reachability and query success rates.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly shows nslookup against 10.200.0.2 returns web0.local–web3.local as 10.200.0.3–10.200.0.6, confirming baseline healthy resolution.

The agent's claims are directly supported by the investigation log (resolv.conf, nslookup/getent results, curl, and ss/netstat showing port 53 listening). Inferences (despite named showing inactive, DNS is functioning because queries are answered and listeners exist) follow logically and the checks cover the essential alternatives.
